'''Deborah Shiu-lan Jin''' ({{lang-zh|s=金秀兰|p=Jīn Xiùlán}}; November 15, 1968 – September 15, 2016) was an American [[physicist]] and fellow with the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST); Professor Adjunct, Department of Physics at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder|University of Colorado]]; and a fellow of the [[JILA]], a NIST joint laboratory with the University of Colorado.<ref name="JILABio">{{cite web|title=Deborah S. Jin|url=https://jila.colorado.edu/faculty/deborah-s-jin|website=JILA, University of Colorado|access-date=3 December 2015|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304083627/https://jila.colorado.edu/faculty/deborah-s-jin}}</ref><ref name="Annenberg">{{cite web|title=Interview with Deborah S. Jin|url=http://www.learner.org/courses/physics/scientist/transcripts/jin.html|website=Annenberg Learner|publisher=Annenberg Foundation|access-date=3 December 2015|archive-date=8 December 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208071253/http://www.learner.org/courses/physics/scientist/transcripts/jin.html}}</ref>

She was considered a pioneer in polar molecular quantum chemistry.<ref name=demarco>{{cite journal |last1=DeMarco |first1=Brian |last2=Bohn |first2=John |last3=Cornell |first3=Eric |title=Deborah S. Jin 1968–2016 |journal=Nature |date=October 2016 |volume=538 |issue=7625 |page=318 |doi=10.1038/538318a |pmid=27762370 |bibcode=2016Natur.538..318D |s2cid=205091045 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Ost/> From 1995 to 1997 she worked with [[Eric Cornell]] and [[Carl Wieman]] at JILA, where she was  involved in some of the earliest studies of dilute gas [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose-Einstein condensates]].<ref name=Mayer/> In 2003 Jin's team at JILA made the first [[fermionic condensate]], a new form of matter.<ref name=NASA>{{cite web|title=A New Form of Matter: II, NASA-supported researchers have discovered a weird new phase of matter called fermionic condensates|url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2004/12feb_fermi/|website=Science News|publisher=Nasa Science|date=February 12, 2004|access-date=July 12, 2017|archive-date=April 2, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190402130901/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2004/12feb_fermi}}</ref> She used magnetic traps and lasers to cool fermionic atomic gases to less than 100 billionths of a degree above zero, successfully demonstrating quantum degeneracy and the formation of a molecular [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose-Einstein condensate]].<ref name=Galvin/><ref name=PRL2004>{{cite journal|last1=Regal|first1=C. A.|last2=Greiner|first2=M.|last3=Jin|first3=D. S.|s2cid=10799388|title=Observation of Resonance Condensation of Fermionic Atom Pairs|journal=Physical Review Letters|date=28 January 2004|volume=92|issue=4|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.040403|arxiv = cond-mat/0401554 |bibcode = 2004PhRvL..92d0403R|pmid=14995356|article-number=040403}}</ref> Jin was frequently mentioned as a strong candidate for the Nobel Prize in Physics.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chang |first1=Kenneth |title=Deborah S. Jin Dies at 47; Physicist Studied Matter in Extreme Cold |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/22/science/deborah-jin-obituary.html |work=The New York Times |date=22 September 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/chadorzel/2015/10/02/predicting-the-nobel-prize-in-physics/|title=Predicting The Nobel Prize In Physics|last=Orzel|first=Chad|work=Forbes|access-date=2017-06-13}}</ref> In 2002, ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized her as one of the 50 most important women in science.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite news|last1=Svitil|first1=Kathy|title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/|access-date=21 December 2014|publisher=Discover|date=13 November 2002}}</ref>

== Biography ==

=== Early life ===
Jin was born in [[Santa Clara County, California]],<ref name="FamSearch">{{cite web|title=California Birth Index, 1905-1995|url=https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VL9C-2S5|website=FamilySearch|access-date=September 19, 2016}}</ref> Jin was one of three children, and grew up in [[Indian Harbour Beach, Florida]].<ref name="WaPo" /> Her father was a physicist and her mother a physicist working as an engineer.<ref name="WaPo" /> Her father Ron Jin was born in [[Fuzhou]] in 1933 and died in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-09-22 |title=一盏过早熄灭的科学明灯 (A beacon of science that was extinguished too early) |url=https://www.sohu.com/a/www.sohu.com/a/114849144_116413 |access-date=2022-05-28 |website=www.sohu.com |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=January 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

=== Education ===
Jin graduated magna cum laude from [[Princeton University]] in 1990, receiving a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in physics after completing a senior thesis titled "A Condensation-Pumped Dilution Refrigerator for Use in Cooling Millimeter Wave Bolometer Detectors".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deborah S. Jin - CV|url=https://jila.colorado.edu/jin/sites/default/files/uploads/CV_Jin.pdf|last=|first=|date=|website=|archive-date=2015-10-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151005042855/https://jila.colorado.edu/jin/sites/default/files/uploads/CV_Jin.pdf}}</ref><ref name=Mayer/><ref>{{Cite book|last=Jin|first=Deborah S.|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/4122253|title=A Condensation-Pumped Dilution Refrigerator for Use in Cooling Millimeter Wave Bolometer Detectors|date=1990|publisher=Princeton, NJ: Department of Physics|language=English}}</ref> She was a recipient of the [[Allen Shenstone|Allen G. Shenstone]] Prize in Physics in 1990.

Jin then studied at the [[University of Chicago]], where she was a [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Graduate Fellow from 1990 to 1993 and received a Ph.D. in physics in 1995, completing a doctoral thesis titled "Experimental Study of the Phase Diagrams of Heavy Fermion Superconductors with Multiple Transitions" under the supervision of [[Thomas Felix Rosenbaum]].<ref name="thesis-jin-1995">{{cite thesis |id={{ProQuest|304247574}} |title=Experimental study of the phase diagrams of heavy fermion superconductors with multiple transitions |date=1995 |publisher=[[The University of Chicago]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Jin |first=Deborah Shiu-lan |oclc=833462117 }}</ref>

=== Scientific contributions ===
After completing her Ph.D., Jin joined [[Eric Allin Cornell|Eric Cornell's]] group at [[JILA]], the Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics in [[Boulder, Colorado|Boulder]], [[Colorado]], as a postdoctoral researcher. This change from condensed matter to atomic physics required her to learn a new set of experimental techniques. Jin joined Cornell's group soon after they achieved the first rubidium [[Bose Einstein condensate|Bose-Einstein condensate]] (BEC), and performed experiments characterizing its properties.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chang |first1=Kenneth |title=Lives: Deborah Jin '90 |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/article/lives-deborah-jin-90 |website=Princeton Alumni Weekly |date=27 January 2017 |access-date=26 July 2019}}</ref>

In 1997, Jin formed her own group at JILA. Within two years, she developed the ability to create the first quantum degenerate gas of fermionic atoms. The work was motivated by earlier studies of BEC's and the ability to cool a dilute gas of atoms to 1 μK. The weak interactions between particles in a BEC led to interesting physics. It was theorized that fermionic atoms would form an analogous state at low enough temperatures, with fermions pairing up in a phenomenon similar to the creation of [[Cooper pair]]s in [[Superconductivity|superconducting]] materials.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Exploring a quantum degenerate gas of fermionic atoms|first1=B.|last1=DeMarco|first2=D. S.|last2=Jin|s2cid=119413726|date=1 December 1998|journal=Physical Review A|volume=58|issue=6|pages=R4267–R4270|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.58.R4267|arxiv=cond-mat/9807406|bibcode=1998PhRvA..58.4267D}}</ref>

The work was complicated by the fact that, unlike [[boson]]s, [[fermion]]s cannot occupy the same quantum state at the same time, due to the [[Pauli exclusion principle]], and are therefore limited with regard to cooling mechanisms. At low enough temperature [[Evaporative cooling (atomic physics)|evaporative cooling]], an important technique used to reach low enough temperature to create the first BEC's, is no longer effective for fermions. To circumvent this issue, Jin and her team cooled potassium-40 atoms in two different magnetic sublevels. This enabled atoms in different sublevels to collide with each other, restoring the efficacy of evaporative cooling. Using this technique, Jin and her group were able to produce a degenerate [[Fermi gas]] at a temperature of about 300 nK, or half the [[Fermi temperature]] of the mixture.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Fermion gas achieves quantum degeneracy|date=5 April 1999|journal=Physics World|volume=12|issue=10|page=5|doi=10.1088/2058-7058/12/10/2}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=DeMarco |first1=B. |last2=Jin |first2=D. S. |title=Onset of Fermi Degeneracy in a Trapped Atomic Gas |journal=Science |date=10 September 1999 |volume=285 |issue=5434 |pages=1703–1706 |doi=10.1126/science.285.5434.1703|pmid=10481000 }}</ref>

In 2003, Jin and her team were the first to condense pairs of fermionic atoms. They directly observed a molecular Bose-Einstein condensate created solely by adjusting the interaction strength in an ultracold Fermi gas of atoms using a [[Feshbach resonance]]. She was able to observe transitions of the gas between a [[BCS theory|Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) state]] and Bose-Einstein condensate.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Greiner|first1=Markus|last2=Regal|first2=Cindy A.|last3=Jin|first3=Deborah S.|s2cid=4348155|title=Emergence of a molecular Bose–Einstein condensate from a Fermi gas|journal=Nature|volume=426|issue=6966|pages=537–540|doi=10.1038/nature02199|bibcode=2003Natur.426..537G|year=2003|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233267|pmid=14647340}}</ref>

In 2008, Jin and her team developed a technique analogous to [[angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy]] (ARPES) which allowed them to measure excitations of their degenerate gas with both energy- and momentum-resolution. They used this approach to study the nature of fermion pairing across the [[BCS-BEC crossover]], the same system her group had first explored in 2003.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=J. T. |last2=Gaebler |first2=J. P. |last3=Jin |first3=D. S. |s2cid=4309856 |title=Using photoemission spectroscopy to probe a strongly interacting Fermi gas |journal=Nature |date=August 2008 |volume=454 |issue=7205 |pages=744–747 |doi=10.1038/nature07172|pmid=18685703 |arxiv=0805.0026 |bibcode=2008Natur.454..744S }}</ref> These experiments provided the first experimental evidence of a [[pseudogap]] in the BCS-BEC crossover.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaebler |first1=J. P. |last2=Stewart |first2=J. T. |last3=Drake |first3=T. E. |last4=Jin |first4=D. S. |last5=Perali |first5=A. |last6=Pieri |first6=P. |last7=Strinati |first7=G. C. |s2cid=119294316 |title=Observation of pseudogap behaviour in a strongly interacting Fermi gas |journal=Nature Physics |date=4 July 2010 |volume=6 |issue=8 |pages=569–573 |doi=10.1038/nphys1709|arxiv=1003.1147 |bibcode=2010NatPh...6..569G }}</ref>

Jin continued to advance the frontiers of ultracold science when she and her colleague, Jun Ye, managed to cool polar molecules that possess a large electric dipole moment to ultracold temperatures, also in 2008. Rather than directly cool polar molecules, they created a gas of ultracold atoms and then transformed them into dipolar molecules in a coherent way. This work led to novel insights regarding the chemical reactions near absolute zero. They were able to observe and control potassium-rubidium (KRb) molecules in the lowest energy state (ground state). They were even able to observe molecules colliding and breaking and forming chemical bonds.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://jila.colorado.edu/yelabs/research/ultracold-molecules|title=Ultracold Molecules - Ye Group|website=jila.colorado.edu}}</ref> Jin's husband, John Bohn, who specialized in the theory of ultracold atomic collisions, collaborated with her on this work.

==Honors and awards==

Jin was an elected  member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (2005)<ref name=Ost/> and Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2007).<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Professor Deborah S. Jin|url=https://www.amacad.org/content/system/search.aspx?s=Deborah+Jin|archive-url=https://archive.today/20160113004050/https://www.amacad.org/content/system/search.aspx?s=Deborah+Jin|archive-date=13 January 2016|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|access-date=3 December 2015}}</ref><ref name=AAASMembers>{{cite web|title=2007 Class of Fellows and Foreign Honorary Members by Class and Section|url=http://2m.com/wp-content/uploads/2M_AAAS-Announces-2007-Class-of-Fellows.pdf|website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=3 December 2015|archive-date=8 December 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208100720/http://2m.com/wp-content/uploads/2M_AAAS-Announces-2007-Class-of-Fellows.pdf}}</ref>

Jin won a number of prestigious awards, including:
* 2000, [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers|Presidential Early Career Award]] in Science and Engineering<ref name="JILABio" />
* 2001, NIST [[Samuel Wesley Stratton Award|Samuel W. Stratton Award]]
* 2002, [[Maria Goeppert-Mayer Award]]<ref name=Mayer>{{cite web|title=2002 Maria Goeppert Mayer Award Recipient Deborah S. Jin|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Jin&first_nm=Deborah&year=2002|website=American Physical Society|access-date=3 December 2015}}</ref>
* 2002, National Academy of Sciences Award for Initiatives in Research
* 2003, [[MacArthur Foundation|MacArthur Fellowship]] "genius grant"<ref name="MacArthur">{{cite web|title=MacArthur Fellows / Meet the Class of 2003 Deborah Jin|url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/710/|website=MacArthur Foundation|access-date=3 December 2015}}</ref>
* 2003, [[Arthur S. Flemming Award]] (Scientific Category)
* 2004, Service to America Medal: Science and the Environment
* 2004, ''[[Scientific American]]'s'' "Research Leader of the Year"<ref name="Holloway">{{cite journal|last1=Holloway|first1=Marguerite|title=Superhot among the Ultracool|journal=Scientific American|volume=291|date=2004|issue=September|pages=40–42|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0904-40|pmid=15376749|bibcode=2004SciAm.291c..40H}}</ref>
* 2005, American Physical Society, [[I. I. Rabi Prize|I.I. Rabi Prize]]
* 2006, Bonfils-Stanton Foundation Award in Science and Medicine
* 2008, [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|The Benjamin Franklin Medal]] in Physics<ref name="Franklin">{{cite web|title=Deborah Jin|url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/deborah-jin|website=The Franklin Institute|date=15 January 2014|access-date=2 December 2015}}</ref>
* 2009, Sigma Xi, The William Proctor Prize for Scientific Achievement
* 2011, Gold Medal, NIST, Department of Commerce
* 2013, L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Award Laureate for North America<ref name="Davidowitz">{{cite news|last1=Davidowitz|first1=Suzie|title=L'OREAL-UNESCO for Women in Science Names Professor Deborah Jin 2013 Laureate for North America|url=http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/loreal-unesco-women-science-names-professor-deborah-jin-2013-laureate-north-america-1716296.htm|access-date=3 December 2015|work=Market Wired|date=October 22, 2012|archive-date=6 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180806180949/http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/loreal-unesco-women-science-names-professor-deborah-jin-2013-laureate-north-america-1716296.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="NewsAfrica">{{cite news|title=Five exceptional women scientists receive L'OREAL-UNESCO Awards|url=http://www.africa-news.eu/immigration-news/immigration-news/world/five-exceptional-women-scientists-receive-loreal-unesco-awards.html|access-date=3 December 2015|work=News Africa|date=8 April 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20160907200456/http://www.africa-news.eu/immigration-news/immigration-news/world/five-exceptional-women-scientists-receive-loreal-unesco-awards.html|archive-date=7 September 2016}}</ref>
* 2014, The [[Institute of Physics Isaac Newton Medal]]<ref name=IOP>{{cite web|title=Institute of Physics announces 2014 award winners|url=http://www.iop.org/news/14/jul/page_63442.html|website=[[Institute of Physics]]|access-date=4 July 2014|archive-date=29 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729031247/http://www.iop.org/news/14/jul/page_63442.html}}</ref>
*2014, [[Comstock Prize in Physics]], "for a recent innovative discovery or investigation in electricity, magnetism, or radiant energy."<ref name=Ost>{{cite web|last1=Ost|first1=Laura|title=JILA/NIST Fellow Deborah Jin to Receive 2014 Comstock Prize in Physics|url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/div689/jin-012914.cfm|newspaper=Nist|date=29 January 2014|access-date=January 29, 2014}}</ref><ref name=Galvin>{{cite news|last1=Galvin|first1=Molly|title=Academy Honors 15 for Major Contributions to Science|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/jan-16-2014-NASawards.html|access-date=3 December 2015|work=News from the National Academy of Sciences|agency=National Academy of Sciences|date=January 16, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208055507/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/jan-16-2014-NASawards.html|archive-date=8 December 2015}}</ref>
*2014, "Most Influential Scientific Minds of 2014," with [[Jun Ye]], released from Thomson Reuters
After she died the [[American Physical Society]] renamed its DAMOP graduate student prize after Deborah Jin to acknowledge her impact in the field of atomic, molecular, and optical physics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/updates/deborah-jin.cfm|title=Deborah Jin's Legacy Honored by DAMOP|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=2017-06-13}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Jin married John Bohn, and had a daughter.<ref name="WaPo" /> Jin died of cancer on September 15, 2016, in Boulder, Colorado.<ref name="WaPo">{{cite news|last=Weil |first=Martin |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/deborah-jin-government-physicist-who-won-macarthur-genius-grant-dies-at-47/2016/09/20/c2deb8ce-7ed9-11e6-8d13-d7c704ef9fd9_story.html |title=Deborah Jin, government physicist who won MacArthur 'genius' grant, dies at 47 |newspaper=The Washington Post|date=20 September 2016|access-date=2016-09-22}}</ref><ref name="JILA">{{cite web|title=Deborah Jin Dies at 47|url=https://jila.colorado.edu/news/deborah-jin-dies-47|website=JILA|access-date=19 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160919232448/https://jila.colorado.edu/news/deborah-jin-dies-47|archive-date=19 September 2016|date=19 September 2016}}</ref>
